newsitem.title: UK: Adapt or risk losing supervisory role, MPs tell BOE.
newsitem.headline: Adapt or risk losing supervisory role, MPs tell BOE.

text.p: Supervision of Britain's banks may have to be removed from the Bank of England unless it can shake off its "old culture" of being too close to the banking industry, parliament's Treasury Committee said on Tuesday.

In a report into the collapse last year of Barings bank, the cross-party committee expressed concern that the BoE, as a former bank itself and a "cheerleader" for the City, might shy away from measures that would displease the banks or impair London's competitiveness.

"The Bank needs to demonstrate that it is able to separate its supervisory activities from its other functions and avoid any possible weakening of its regulatory effectiveness due to its proximity to the day-to-day banking market.
"Otherwise it may be that in order to bring about the necessary cultural change banking supervision will have to be taken away from the Bank of England," the MPs said.

Barings, Britain's oldest merchant bank, collapsed last year under the weight of more than $1 billion in speculative losses chalked up by Singapore-based derivatives trader Nick Leeson, now serving a jail sentence in the south-east Asian city state.
The MPs said it was not apparent that Britain's banks had earned the "soft touch" in supervision provided by the BoE.
They also said they were worried that, despite recent changes at senior level in the central bank, the existing climate will persist.
"The Bank has tried in the past to assure us that a new era has commenced in its supervisory wing and so we are concerned that this may be another false dawn," the report said.

Evidence collected by the committee suggests that the Bank's claim to have become a much sharper, hands-on supervisor did not apply in the case of Barings "and we are concerned that the laudable aims the Bank currently outlines may similarly fall by the wayside," the MPs said.

The MPs said the Barings case illustrated "considerable weaknesses" and "obvious shortcomings" in the BoE's supervisory regime in areas such as the evaluation of internal controls at banks, internal communication at the BoE itself, and the application of its existing rules.

The committee welcomed the BoE's decision to pump more resources into banking supervision and urged it to ensure that the type of laxity of management unearthed at Barings could not go undetected in future.
The Treasury panel said the Barings case also highlighted inadequate cooperation among international regulators.

It called on the government to set a good example by legislating to ensure there are no barriers to the exchange of information, which it said may be necessary if the concept of a lead regulator is to be successful at international level.
"There are clearly improvements in relationships and communication channels between regulators still to be made at an international level.

"Unfortunately, it appears that it is not yet the first instinct of all regulators who have a concern about an institution to contact the other regulators involved and not just the institution itself," the report said.
